Author Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India; Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India
Publication Title: 2026 International Conference on Machine Intelligence for GeoAnalytics and Remote Sensing (MIGARS)
Abstract: Accurate building footprint extraction from airborne LiDAR and high-resolution imagery is critical for urban flood modeling and digital twin applications. However, existing methods face challenges due to noise, occlusions, incomplete structures, and complex urban geometry. Traditional geometric approaches lack scalability and robustness, while deep learning methods, despite high accuracy, require large annotated datasets and often fail to preserve structural consistency in dense urban environments. This paper proposes a semantic and geometryaware hybrid framework that integrates data-driven and modeldriven strategies. The approach employs the Segment Anything Model (SAM3), a prompt-driven foundation segmentation model, on RGB orthoimage for initial building region proposals, followed by refinement using competing prompts to explicitly separate buildings from vegetation. The resulting masks are further processed through geometric boundary extraction to obtain consistent building footprints under noisy and incomplete conditions. The extracted footprints are then integrated with LiDAR point cloud data for height estimation and 3D reconstruction. Compared to purely deep learning methods, the proposed framework improves boundary accuracy and geometric consistency while reducing dependence on large labeled datasets. Experimental results demonstrate strong agreement with human annotations, with IoU values typically ranging from 0.80 to 0.93 and F1-scores exceeding 0.90 for most buildings, while also highlighting failure cases under dense vegetation.

Abstract: Building footprint extraction is a fundamental task in photogrammetry, remote sensing, and computer vision. Recent image-based methods have achieved remarkable progress in extracting vectorized footprints from high-resolution optical imagery. However, optical imagery is inherently susceptible to occlusions, perspective distortions, and residual relief displacement, yielding incomplete or misaligned extractions. Furthermore, the lack of explicit elevation information limits its direct applicability to level of detail building modeling. To overcome these fundamental limitations, we present PCFootprint, the first large-scale public dataset dedicated to building footprint extraction from real aerial laser scanning point clouds. Significantly surpassing existing LiDAR-based datasets in scale, PCFootprint comprises 33 000 tiles featuring systematically aligned vectorized annotations across diverse urban and rural landscapes. Furthermore, in order to push the robustness of future algorithms, we construct a unique 3000-tile cross-domain benchmark to evaluate model generalization across unseen geographic regions. Comprehensive evaluations of mainstream methods reveal critical unresolved challenges in the 3-D domain, including high intraclass variance, severe data imbalance, and noise in complex geospatial environments. As a comprehensive public benchmark, we believe PCFootprint will facilitate future research in 3-D building modeling, urban scene understanding, and geospatial analysis.

Abstract: Wide-area 3-D data generation in complex urban environments frequently necessitates the integration of multisource observations acquired from both aerial and terrestrial platforms, such as aerial surveys and mobile mapping systems. The resulting minimal spatial overlap, due to the heterogeneous sensor lines of sight, makes accurate registration highly challenging and typically requires substantial manual intervention. Furthermore, the registration process is further complicated by scale ambiguities inherent in the street-view data (e.g., GPS-denied or GPS-weak). In this work, we present a robust cross-view registration framework based on the assumption that building façade structures remain consistent across aerial and street-view datasets. A pair of dual gravity lines (DGLs) across cross-view datasets serves as a minimal solver for estimating the similarity transformation, offering a simpler and more efficient solution compared with standard methods that require three-point correspondence. Furthermore, we incorporate a novel scale-invariant similarity metric into the random sample consensus (RANSAC) framework, enabling more reliable estimation even under significant scale differences. We also released a cross-view registration benchmark, named Cross-View Urban (CV-Urban), adopting two public datasets: ISPRS Multiplatform and ULTRRA Challenge datasets, covering three cities with areas totaling 366 388 m2. It is proposed to comprehensively evaluate the registration methods on cross-view scenarios with various occlusion (average 10%), scale variations, and noisy levels. Extensive experiments on the CV-Urban dataset show that our method effectively aligns cross-view datasets, even in cases of extremely limited overlap and substantial scale differences. Abstract: Background: The use of point clouds to perform quality control (QC) of prefabricated structural systems is growing markedly. The sustained application of point clouds on construction projects at scale, however, requires reliable and automated frameworks to foster practicality. Literature Review: Existing solutions seldom incorporate the impact of instrument artifacts, construction errors, and complex element geometries, rendering the frameworks error-prone and sensitive to thresholds, outliers, and missing data. More specifically, current methods: 1) are not generalizable to any freeform element; 2) rely on local primitives, which increases runtime and threshold subjectivity; 3) do not formulate the point cloud to model fitting based on geometric distance; and 4) do not incorporate a dedicated outlier detection to explicitly handle large outliers. Methodology: This study presents, scan-to-QC, a generic solution for automatic QC of prefabricated elements with non-analytic cross-sections using point clouds. The framework addresses the current state-of-the-art limitations (above) by providing a generic, direct artificial-intelligence (AI)-based geometric distance fitting robust to outliers. The proposed approach introduces four new algorithms to: 1) represent the cross-sectional boundaries of elements with trigonometric polynomials, 2) perform orthogonal fitting of points to these polynomials, 3) remove outlying observations through robust concentration steps (CS), and 4) perform assembly verification of prefabricated elements in construction projects. As the convergence of CS depends on the initial fitting parameters, the performances of seven deterministic, heuristic, and AI-based (i.e., metaheuristic and global computational intelligence-based) optimization strategies to recover these parameters were evaluated on point clouds of five common prefabricated elements with complex geometries. The comparative analysis considered factors such as the fit quality, object detection accuracy, and computation runtime. Results and Conclusions: Among these methods, the Particle Swarm (PS) achieved the best results, significantly outperforming Simulated Annealing, Bayesian, and Genetic Algorithm. Furthermore, by fine-tuning the swarm size, the PS attained 99% and 96% accuracies in object detection and fitting quality, respectively. Finally, the calibrated PS algorithm was applied to the point cloud of a real-world prefabricated spaceframe structure, yielding 98.5% reliability in nodal coordinate estimation compared to the ground truth.

Abstract: Geometrically robust 3D watermarking is a practical mechanism for protecting digital graphical assets used in CAD/CAM, entertainment pipelines, digital twins, and additive manufacturing. However, many works still equate “robustness” with survival under routine processing (e.g., smoothing or decimation) and rarely specify what an adaptive adversary can observe, query, or optimize. Building on a review of spectral-geometric invariants under realistic 3D acquisition distortions, this paper proposes a security-aware blueprint for evaluating and designing robust 3D watermarks under explicit threat assumptions. We contribute three methodological layers. First, we formalize a threat model capturing representation changes (mesh ↔ point cloud), acquisition-reconstruction loops, oracle access to embedding or detection services, collusion across many samples, and a utility constraint that prevents trivial “removal by destruction.” Second, we introduce gamebased security definitions for removal, forgery, ambiguity, payload manipulation, and key recovery, with measurable adversarial advantages at a fixed detector operating point (controlled false-alarm rate). Third, we propose a parameterized attack taxonomy and a reproducible attacklibrary interface supporting composed attacks, adaptive score minimization, and standardized metadata logging. The resulting protocol reports both robustness curves (TPR/BER vs. attack strength) and security curves (e.g., key-recovery advantage vs. the number of observed assets). We illustrate the blueprint on spectral-geometric invariant watermarking, highlighting eigenbasis drift under remeshing/reconstruction and key-leakage risks under key reuse.

Abstract: The lower 12 GHz band (12.2–12.7 GHz) has emerged as a key candidate for future 6G deployments, yet its use is constrained by the need to protect highly sensitive passive Fixed Satellite Service receive-only Earth Stations (FSS-ES), which neither transmit nor provide interference feedback. This absence of incumbent sensing or reporting fundamentally limits conventional dynamic spectrum sharing approaches and creates a challenging cognitive networking problem. In order to address this problem, this paper presents DigiCaM, a Digital Twin–assisted cognitive spectrum sharing framework that enables feedback-free coexistence between 6G macro base stations (MBSs) and passive FSS-ES receivers in the 12 GHz band. We formulate the coexistence problem as a constrained optimization and show it is NP-hard. To address this, we develop (i) a greedy algorithm with provable (1 − 1/e) approximation guarantees via monotone submodular maximization, and (ii) a recurrent deep reinforcement learning (R-DRL) approach with Lagrangian duality to enforce regulatory interference constraints while adapting to dynamic network and environmental conditions. Extensive evaluations in a realistic MBS deployment in Blacksburg, VA demonstrate that DigiCaM achieves interference estimation accuracy comparable to high-fidelity ray tracing while reducing computation time by orders of magnitude. Abstract: Urban scene reconstruction plays a critical role in applications such as autonomous navigation and digital twin systems. As a key technique for scene reconstruction, multiview stereo (MVS) has made significant progress in general scenarios. However, it remains fragile in complex urban environments. Challenges such as weak textures, dense occlusion, depth adhesions, and illumination variations severely impair the effectiveness of traditional photometric and geometric consistency constraints, leading to unstable depth estimation and topological artifacts. To address these issues, we propose StableMVS, a robust depth estimation method that integrates semantic priors, structural cues, and perturbation-aware learning. Specifically, epistemic-structural prior infusion introduces cognitive priors and semantic layout from large vision models to enhance depth inference in ambiguous regions. Morphology-encoded depth field optimization (MeDF) leverages boundary-aware morphology to suppress distortions and topological artifacts near depth discontinuities. Furthermore, diffusion-propelled feature fidelity learning adopts a disturbance–restoration paradigm that improves feature stability under real-world perturbations such as lighting shifts and sensor noise. These components collectively form a unified framework that bridges global understanding with local consistency, yielding structurally coherent and resilient depth estimation across challenging urban scenarios. Experiments on multiple public datasets show that StableMVS achieves competitive accuracy under low-texture, occlusion, and illumination variation conditions, validating its effectiveness for real-world MVS applications. Abstract: Object detection is a task in computer vision that involves detecting instances of visual objects of a particular class in digital images. Numerous computer vision tasks highly depend on object detection such as instance segmentation, image captioning and object tracking. A major purpose of object detection is to develop computational models that provide inputs crucial to computer vision applications. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have recently become popular due to their key roles in enabling object detection. However, the performance of CNNs is largely dependent upon the quality and quantity of training datasets, which are often difficult to obtain in real-world applications. In order to ensure the robustness of such models, it is vital that training instances are provided under various randomized conditions. These conditions are typically a combination of a variety of factors, including lighting conditions, object location, the presence of multiple objects in the scene, varieties of backgrounds, and the angle of the camera. In particular, companies, depending on their applications (such as fault detection, anomaly detection, condition monitoring, predictive quality and so on), require specialized models for their custom products and so always face difficulties in providing a large number of randomized conditioned instances of their objects. The primary reason is that the process of capturing randomized conditioned images of real objects is usually costly, time-consuming, and challenging in practice. Due to the efficiency gained so far via the use of synthetic data for training such systems, synthetic data has recently attracted considerable attention. This paper presents an end-to-end synthetic data generation method for building a robust object detection model for customized products using NVIDIA Omniverse and CNNs. In this paper, we demonstrate and evaluate our contribution to the modeling of chess pieces, where a total accuracy of 98.8 % was obtained.

Abstract: Automated semantic segmentation of the three-dimensional (3D) built environment remains a fundamental challenge in 3D computer vision and urban perception, supporting applications ranging from autonomous navigation to urban infrastructure management. Existing benchmarks are primarily focused on highway environments, limiting their ability to capture the geometric ambiguity and spatial complexity of mixed-use urban scenes. To overcome this limitation, ITU-Campus3D is introduced as a large-scale mobile laser-scanning dataset containing over 239 million annotated points collected in a complex campus environment. In addition to dataset construction, a robust benchmarking framework is established that incorporates an adaptive spatial split strategy and tile-level rare-class balancing to mitigate spatial correlation and severe class imbalance during evaluation. Using this framework, five state-of-the-art segmentation architectures, spanning point-based, voxel-based, and hybrid paradigms, are systematically evaluated. While modern architectures achieve competitive overall performance, reaching a mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) of 73.18% with an overall accuracy of about 91.55%, conventional evaluation metrics are shown to conceal failures in rare semantic classes. To explicitly assess segmentation reliability under long-tailed class distributions, the rare-class metric  $\text {mIoU}_{\text {rare}}$  is introduced. The evaluation reveals an approximately 8.00% performance gap between the mIoU and  $\text {mIoU}_{\text {rare}}$ , highlighting a critical limitation of current urban scene understanding models. Further analysis indicates that segmentation errors on structurally sparse urban objects, such as signs and poles, are largely driven by geometric similarity, occlusion, and complex neighborhood complexity. By explicitly exposing these failure modes, ITU-Campus3D serves as a diagnostic benchmark that advances urban semantic segmentation beyond aggregate accuracy metrics toward reliable real-world deployment.

Abstract: Recent statistics and studies show that the loss generated by insider threats is much higher than that generated by external attacks. Abstract: Depth estimation is a critical problem in robotics applications especially autonomous driving. Abstract: As an efficient and inexpensive acquisition platform, Autonomous Aerial Vehicles (AAVs) are particularly suitable for image acquisition in 3D ship reconstruction tasks.
